1.o: This book begins with the laws concerning sacrifices, of which the most ancient were the burnt-offerings, about which God gives Moses instructions in this chapter. Orders are here given how that sort of sacrifice must be managed. I. If it was a bullock out of the herd, ver. 3-9. II. If it was a sheep or goat, a lamb or kid, out of the flock, ver. 10-13. III. If it was a turtle-dove or a young pigeon, ver. 14-17.
1.i: Leviticus opens with the first three kinds of gifts brought to the newly finished tent, and each one has its own picture of what it means to belong to God.
1.p: Lord, You ask for our whole selves, our daily work, and our company. Teach us to bring all three with glad hearts. Amen.
1.l: Say a thank-you to God today for something you eat, and share some of it with someone else.
q: Neither grief nor mere pleasure belonged on the altar. What do you bring to God that is only one extreme?

2.o: In this chapter we have the law concerning the meat-offering. I. The matter of it; whether of raw flour with oil and incense (ver. 1), or baked in the oven (ver. 4), or upon a plate (ver. 5, 6), or in a frying pan, ver. 7. II. The management of it, of the flour (ver. 2, 3), of the cakes, ver. 8-10. III. Some particular rules concerning it, That leaven and honey must never be admitted (ver. 11, 12), and salt never omitted in the meat-offering, ver. 13. IV.
2.i: Leviticus opens with the first three kinds of gifts brought to the newly finished tent, and each one has its own picture of what it means to belong to God.
2.p: Lord, You ask for our whole selves, our daily work, and our company. Teach us to bring all three with glad hearts. Amen.
2.l: Say a thank-you to God today for something you eat, and share some of it with someone else.
q: Neither grief nor mere pleasure belonged on the altar. What do you bring to God that is only one extreme?

3.o: In this chapter we have the law concerning the peace-offerings, whether they were, I. Of the heard, a bullock or a heifer, ver. 1-5. Or, II. Of the flock, either a lamb (ver. 6-11) or a goat, ver. 12-17. The ordinances concerning each of these are much the same, yet they are repeated, to show the care we ought to take that all our services be done according to the appointment and the pleasure God takes in the services that are so performed.
3.i: Leviticus opens with the first three kinds of gifts brought to the newly finished tent, and each one has its own picture of what it means to belong to God.
3.p: Lord, You ask for our whole selves, our daily work, and our company. Teach us to bring all three with glad hearts. Amen.
3.l: Say a thank-you to God today for something you eat, and share some of it with someone else.
q: Neither grief nor mere pleasure belonged on the altar. What do you bring to God that is only one extreme?

4.o: This chapter is concerning the sin-offering, which was properly intended to make atonement for a sin committed through ignorance, I. By the priest himself, ver. 1-12. Or, II. By the whole congregation, ver. 13-21. Or, III. By a ruler, ver. 22-26. Or, IV. By a private person, ver. 27, &c.
4.i: Leviticus 4 to 6 deal with wrongs done by mistake or in a moment of weakness, and with the repayment that must go with an offering.
4.p: Lord, thank You for making a way to be forgiven. Give us courage to put right what we have done wrong. Amen.
4.l: If you have hurt someone, say sorry and fix what you can today.
q: Touching something unclean was only a ceremonial matter, but neglecting to wash afterward showed carelessness. Where might small neglects be telling you something?

5.o: This chapter, and part of the next, concern the trespass-offering. The difference between this and the sin-offering lay not so much in the sacrifices themselves, and the management of them, as in the occasions of the offering of them. They were both intended to make atonement for sin; but the former was more general, this applied to some particular instances. Observe what is here said, I. Concerning the trespass. If a man sin, 1. In concealing his knowledge, when he is adjured, ver. 1. 2.
5.i: Leviticus 4 to 6 deal with wrongs done by mistake or in a moment of weakness, and with the repayment that must go with an offering.
5.p: Lord, thank You for making a way to be forgiven. Give us courage to put right what we have done wrong. Amen.
5.l: If you have hurt someone, say sorry and fix what you can today.
q: Touching something unclean was only a ceremonial matter, but neglecting to wash afterward showed carelessness. Where might small neglects be telling you something?

6.o: The first seven verses of this chapter might fitly have been added to the foregoing chapter, being a continuation of the law of the trespass-offering, and the putting of other cases in which it was to be offered; and with this end the instructions God gave concerning the several kinds of sacrifices that should be offered: and then at v. 8 (which in the original begins a new section of the law) he comes to appoint the several rites and ceremonies concerning these sacrifices which had not been mentioned before. I.
6.i: Leviticus 4 to 6 deal with wrongs done by mistake or in a moment of weakness, and with the repayment that must go with an offering.
6.p: Lord, thank You for making a way to be forgiven. Give us courage to put right what we have done wrong. Amen.
6.l: If you have hurt someone, say sorry and fix what you can today.
q: Touching something unclean was only a ceremonial matter, but neglecting to wash afterward showed carelessness. Where might small neglects be telling you something?

7.o: Here is, I. The law of the trespass-offering (ver. 1-7), with some further directions concerning the burnt-offering and the meat-offering, ver. 8-10. II. The law of the peace-offering. The eating of it (ver. 11-21), on which occasion the prohibition of eating fat or blood is repeated (ver. 22-27), and the priests' share of it, ver. 28-34. III. The conclusion of those institutions, ver. 35, &c.
7.i: Leviticus 6 and 7 give the priests the instructions behind the offerings: how to tend the fire, who eats what, and how long a shared meal lasts.
7.p: Lord, keep the fire of our love for You burning, in the night as well as in the day. Amen.
7.l: Do a small job today that no one will notice, and do it well, for God.
q: The burnt offering meant giving oneself, soul and body, to God. What would it look like to keep that fire lit on an ordinary morning?

8.o: This chapter gives us an account of the solemn consecration of Aaron and his sons to the priest's office. I. It was done publicly, and the congregation was called together to be witnesses of it, ver. 1-4. II. It was done exactly according to God's appointment, ver. 5. 1. They were washed and dressed, ver. 6-9, 13. 2. The tabernacle and the utensils of it were anointed, and then the priests, ver. 10-12. 3. A sin-offering was offered for them, ver. 14-17. 4. A burnt-offering, ver. 18-21. 5.
8.i: Leviticus 8 is the day the instructions of Exodus 28 and 29 are carried out, one step at a time, with the whole community watching.
8.p: Lord, You set people apart to serve You. Make us faithful in the small steps of obedience. Amen.
8.l: Do something this week because God asked you to, even if no one else would notice.
q: The priests had to stay at the tent for seven days and not leave. When have you had to stay with something until it was finished?

9.o: Aaron and his sons, having been solemnly consecrated to the priesthood, are in this chapter entering upon the execution of their office, the very next day after their consecration was completed. I. Moses (no doubt by direction from God) appoints a meeting between God and his priests, as the representatives of his people, ordering them to attend him, and assuring them that he would appear to them, ver. 1-7. II. The meeting is held according to the appointment. 1.
9.i: Leviticus 9 and 10 move from the joy of the first worship at the tent to a sudden sorrow, and ask what it means that God is holy.
9.p: Lord, You are holy. Teach us to come to You in the way You have shown, with joy and with reverence. Amen.
9.l: Ask a grown-up to read the next part of this story with you, and talk about what it means to be careful with holy things.
q: The nearness they had been given bred contempt for the One they served. When does being close to something good make you careless with it?

10.o: The story of this chapter is as sad an interruption to the institutions of the levitical law as that of the golden calf was to the account of the erecting of the tabernacle. Here is, I. The sin and death of Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, ver. 1, 2. II. The quieting of Aaron under this sore affliction, ver. 3. III. Orders given and observed about the funeral and mourning, ver. 4-7. IV. A command to the priests not to drink wine when they went in to minister, ver. 8-11. V.
10.i: Leviticus 9 and 10 move from the joy of the first worship at the tent to a sudden sorrow, and ask what it means that God is holy.
10.p: Lord, You are holy. Teach us to come to You in the way You have shown, with joy and with reverence. Amen.
10.l: Ask a grown-up to read the next part of this story with you, and talk about what it means to be careful with holy things.
q: The nearness they had been given bred contempt for the One they served. When does being close to something good make you careless with it?

11.o: The ceremonial law is described by the apostle (Heb. ix. 9, 10) to consist, not only "in gifts and sacrifices," which hitherto have been treated of in this book, but "in meats, and drinks, and divers washings" from ceremonial uncleanness, the laws concerning which begin with this chapter, which puts a difference between some sorts of flesh-meat and others, allowing some to be eaten as clean and forbidding others as unclean. "There is one kind of flesh of men."
11.i: Leviticus 11 lists the animals Israel could and could not eat, and gives the reason in a single line: be holy, for I am holy.
11.p: Lord, You made everything we eat. Make us holy, as You are holy, in how we live and how we eat. Amen.
11.l: Before a meal today, remember that everything we eat is a gift, and thank God for it.
q: Every pot in Jerusalem would one day be holy to the Lord. What ordinary thing in your day could be set apart to him?

12.o: After the laws concerning clean and unclean food come the laws concerning clean and unclean persons; and the first is in this chapter concerning the ceremonial uncleanness of women in child-birth, ver. 1-5. And concerning their purification from that uncleanness, ver. 6, &c.
12.i: Leviticus 12 and 15 treat the ordinary events of the body, and ask what it means for a community to live with God in its midst.
12.p: Lord, You dwell among Your people. Keep us from taking Your nearness lightly, and thank You for welcoming us. Amen.
12.l: Wash your hands before you pray or eat today, and remember how close God is to you.
q: What reminds you that you live near something holy?

13.o: The next ceremonial uncleanness is that of the leprosy, concerning which the law was very large and particular; we have the discovery of it in this chapter, and the cleansing of the leper in the next. Scarcely any one thing in all the levitical law takes up so much room as this. I. Rules are here given by which the priest must judge whether the man had the leprosy or no, according as the symptom was that appeared. 1. If it was a swelling, a scab, or a bright spot, ver. 1-17. 2. If it was a bile, ver. 18-23. 3.
13.s: When the Skin Was Not Well
13.i: Leviticus 13 and 14 describe how the priest examined skin problems, mildew, and what happened when a person got well.
13.p: Lord, You cared for the sick and the shut-out. Make us people who welcome the lonely back. Amen.
13.l: Do something kind today for someone who is sick or left out, even if it is just a card or a call.
q: Uncleanness cut a person off from company for a time. Who is cut off from company where you live, and what would it take to bring them back in?

14.o: The former chapter directed the priests how to convict a leper of ceremonial uncleanness. No prescriptions are given for his cure; but, when God had cured him, the priests are in this chapter directed how to cleanse him. The remedy here is only adapted to the ceremonial part of his disease; but the authority Christ gave to his ministers was to cure the lepers, and so to cleanse them. We have here, I. The solemn declaration of the leper's being clean, with the significant ceremony attending it, ver. 1-9. II.
14.s: When the Skin Was Not Well
14.i: Leviticus 13 and 14 describe how the priest examined skin problems, mildew, and what happened when a person got well.
14.p: Lord, You cared for the sick and the shut-out. Make us people who welcome the lonely back. Amen.
14.l: Do something kind today for someone who is sick or left out, even if it is just a card or a call.
q: Uncleanness cut a person off from company for a time. Who is cut off from company where you live, and what would it take to bring them back in?

15.o: In this chapter we have laws concerning other ceremonial uncleannesses contracted either by bodily disease like that of the leper, or some natural incidents, and this either, I. In men, ver. 1-18. Or, II. In women, ver. 19-33. We need not be at all curious in explaining these antiquated laws, it is enough if we observe the general intention; but we have need to be very cautious lest sin take occasion by the commandment to become more exceedingly sinful; and exceedingly sinful it is when lust is kindled by sparks…
15.i: Leviticus 12 and 15 treat the ordinary events of the body, and ask what it means for a community to live with God in its midst.
15.p: Lord, You dwell among Your people. Keep us from taking Your nearness lightly, and thank You for welcoming us. Amen.
15.l: Wash your hands before you pray or eat today, and remember how close God is to you.
q: What reminds you that you live near something holy?

16.o: In this chapter we have the institution of the annual solemnity of the day of atonement, or expiation, which had as much gospel in it as perhaps any of the appointments of the ceremonial law, as appears by the reference the apostle makes to it, Heb. ix. 7, &c. We had before divers laws concerning sin-offerings for particular persons, and to be offered upon particular occasions; but this is concerning the stated sacrifice, in which the whole nation was interested.
16.i: Leviticus 16 describes the one day a year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, and a goat carried the people's wrongs into the wilderness.
16.p: Lord, You provided a way for our wrongs to be carried far away. Thank You for Jesus, our High Priest. Amen.
16.l: Take a quiet five minutes today to tell God about something you are sorry for, and hear Him say you are forgiven.
q: Christ needed no assistant or substitute in making atonement. What are you still trying to add to it?

17.o: After the law concerning the atonement to be made for all Israel by the high priest, at the tabernacle, with the blood of bulls and goats, in this chapter we have two prohibitions necessary for the preservation of the honour of that atonement. I. That no sacrifice should be offered by any other than the priests, nor anywhere but at the door of the tabernacle, and this upon pain of death, ver. 1-9. II. That no blood should be eaten, and this under the same penalty, ver. 10, &c.
17.i: Leviticus 17 teaches that blood is the life of a creature, and gives one of the Bible's clearest reasons for the sacrifices.
17.p: Lord, You are the giver of life. Teach us to honor every life, and thank You for the life of Jesus given for us. Amen.
17.l: Thank God today for the gift of life, and treat a living thing with care.
q: Worship gone private invented gods of its own. Where does your faith need a shared altar and not just your own?

18.o: Here is, I. A general law against all conformity to the corrupt usages of the heathen, ver. 1-5. II. Particular laws, 1. Against incest, ver. 6-18. 2. Against beastly lusts, and barbarous idolatries, ver. 19-23. III. The enforcement of these laws from the ruin of the Canaanites, ver. 24-30.
18.i: Leviticus 18 and 20 set out God's boundaries for a people who had just left Egypt and were about to enter Canaan.
18.p: Lord, You called Your people out of Egypt and into Your own ways. Keep us from copying what harms, and make us people others can trust. Amen.
18.l: Ask a grown-up what it means to be different in a good way, and think of one way you can be.
q: What old habit have you kept as a relic?

19.o: Some ceremonial precepts there are in this chapter, but most of them are moral. One would wonder that when some of the lighter matters of the law are greatly enlarged upon (witness two long chapters concerning the leprosy) many of the weightier matters are put into a little compass: divers of the single verses of this chapter contain whole laws concerning judgment and mercy; for these are things which are manifest in every man's conscience; men's own thoughts are able to explain these, and to comment upon them. I.
19.i: Leviticus 19 takes the command to be holy and turns it into a list of everyday actions, from the harvest to the marketplace to the way a person speaks.
19.p: Lord, You are holy. Make us holy in the fields and the workplace and the home, and teach us to love our neighbors as ourselves. Amen.
19.l: Do one thing today for a neighbor that no one has asked you to do.
q: The God of truth requires truth in the tongue. Where do you shade the truth in everyday bargaining?

20.o: The laws which before were made are in this chapter repeated and penalties annexed to them, that those who would not be deterred from sin by the fear of God might be deterred from it by the fear of punishment. If we will not avoid such and such practices because the law has made them sin (and it is most acceptable when we go on that principle of religion), surely we shall avoid them when the law has made them death, from a principle of self-preservation. In this chapter we have, I.
20.i: Leviticus 18 and 20 set out God's boundaries for a people who had just left Egypt and were about to enter Canaan.
20.p: Lord, You called Your people out of Egypt and into Your own ways. Keep us from copying what harms, and make us people others can trust. Amen.
20.l: Ask a grown-up what it means to be different in a good way, and think of one way you can be.
q: What old habit have you kept as a relic?

21.o: This chapter might borrow its title from Mal. ii. 1, "And now, O you priests, this commandment is for you." It is a law obliging priests with the utmost care and jealousy to preserve the dignity of their priesthood. I. The inferior priests are here charged both concerning their mourning and concerning their marriages and their children, ver. 1-9. II. The high priest is restrained more than any of them, ver. 10-15. III. Neither the one nor the other must have any blemish, ver. 16, &c.
21.i: Leviticus 21 and 22 add stricter rules for the priests and for the offerings, because those who stand closest to God are most responsible for how they live and what they bring.
21.p: Lord, You are holy, and You make us holy. Keep our hands and hearts clean for Your service. Amen.
21.l: Give your best effort to one thing today, instead of just the leftovers of your time.
q: To eat the holy things in uncleanness was to add to guilt, not lessen it. When has treating something sacred lightly cost you more than it should have?

22.o: In this chapter we have divers laws concerning the priests and sacrifices all for the preserving of the honour of the sanctuary. I. That the priests should not eat the holy things in their uncleanness, ver. 1-9. II. That no stranger who did not belong to some family of the priests should eat of the holy things (ver. 10-13), and, if he did it unwittingly, he must make restitution,, ver. 14-16. III. That the sacrifices which were offered must be without blemish, ver. 17-25. IV.
22.i: Leviticus 21 and 22 add stricter rules for the priests and for the offerings, because those who stand closest to God are most responsible for how they live and what they bring.
22.p: Lord, You are holy, and You make us holy. Keep our hands and hearts clean for Your service. Amen.
22.l: Give your best effort to one thing today, instead of just the leftovers of your time.
q: To eat the holy things in uncleanness was to add to guilt, not lessen it. When has treating something sacred lightly cost you more than it should have?

23.o: Hitherto the levitical law had been chiefly conversant about holy persons, holy things, and holy places; in this chapter we have the institution of holy times, many of which had been mentioned occasionally before, but here they are all put together, only the new moons are not mentioned. All the rest of the feasts of the Lord are, I. The weekly feast of the sabbath, ver. 3. II. The yearly feasts, 1. The passover, and the feast of unleavened bread (ver.
23.i: Leviticus 23 sets out the calendar of Israel's year: the Sabbath, three harvest feasts, and a solemn day of forgiveness.
23.p: Lord, You gave Your people days to rest, remember, and rejoice. Teach us to keep time with You. Amen.
23.l: Plan something special to do this week with your family, a meal or a walk, and say thank you to God while you do it.
q: The year was built around giving thanks at every harvest. What do you mark as a season of thanks, and how?

24.o: In this chapter we have, I. A repetition of the laws concerning the lamps and the show-bread, ver. 1-9. II. A violation of the law against blasphemy, with the imprisonment, trial, condemnation, and execution, of the blasphemer, ver. 10-14, with ver. 23. III. The law against blasphemy reinforced (ver. 15, 16), with sundry other laws, ver. 17, &c.
24.s: Lamp, Bread, and a Hard Case
24.i: Leviticus 24 puts two quiet duties, the lamp and the bread, next to a painful case about how God's name is treated.
24.p: Lord, Your name is holy. Help us to speak of You with honor, and to treat everyone with the same fairness. Amen.
24.l: Say God's name with respect today, and notice when other people use it carelessly.
q: The offender's evil manners produced good laws. What good rule in your own home or work began with someone's mistake?

25.o: The law of this chapter concerns the lands and estates of the Israelites in Canaan, the occupying and transferring of which were to be under the divine direction, as well as the management of religious worship; for, as the tabernacle was a holy house, so Canaan was a holy land; and upon that account, as much as any thing, it was the glory of all lands. In token of a peculiar title which God had to this land, and a right to dispose of it, he appointed, I.
25.i: Leviticus 25 sets up a rhythm of rest and release that reaches into the soil, the family land, and the shackles of debt.
25.p: Lord, the earth is Yours. Teach us to rest, to forgive debts, and to set people free, as You have set us free. Amen.
25.l: Forgive a small debt today, or give back something you have been holding on to.
q: Land was priced by how many years remained until it went home. What would change if we valued things by how long we get to keep them?

26.o: This chapter is a solemn conclusion of the main body of the levitical law. The precepts that follow in this and the following book either relate to some particular matters or are repetitions and explications of the foregoing institutions.
26.i: Leviticus 26 closes the laws of the book with two roads, one of blessing and one of warning, and a promise that God does not give up.
26.p: Lord, You keep Your covenant even when we fail. Draw us back when we wander, and remember Your promises to us. Amen.
26.l: Think of one good promise God has made, and thank Him for it today.
q: Where is your heart still closed to what God is showing you?

27.o: The last verse of the foregoing chapter seemed to close up the statute-book; yet this chapter is added as an appendix. Having given laws concerning instituted services, here he directs concerning vows and voluntary services, the free-will offerings of their mouth.
27.s: What Is Promised to the Lord
27.i: Leviticus ends with rules for keeping promises made to God, and for the tenth that belongs to Him.
27.p: Lord, everything we have is Yours. Help us to keep the promises we make to You and to others. Amen.
27.l: Keep a small promise today, and do exactly what you said you would do.
q: The law did not invent vows, it regulated them. What promise have you made lightly that you should keep, or honestly bring back?
